Below are more detailed notes, which is not requested by user. The probabilities will not be improved by taking notes into account. Before constructing the given posteriors I generated simulated forecasts from reasonable ("reasonable" may only mae sense to users of PG_allocated_eps forecasts) parameterization of what I call the "increasing likelihood ratio" model. In a nutshell, the main idea is that the total "likelihood ratio" in favor of an event occurring grows monotonically over time, and "likelihood ratio" is used instead of the probability directly primarily to simplify prior generation. If you're even remotely interested in learning more about the model, check out the Forecast_Allocation notebook in the Forecast_Allocations repo on Github.

In this case, I used the onset date of 2024-09-19 and the completion dates of December 31st of either 2026 or 2030 as my parameters. To get a sense of realistic parameters I first reviewed the number of reported solutions for Millennium problems indicated through various online sources. This effectively becomes an intuitive reported rate of resolution for these problems. Using the first parameter, we can cap low values on our parameter range by asking: What is the historic rate of resolution? The domain of our estimated odds ratio can be parameterized by asking: What if one problem gets solved every 1000 years, and is that practically low enough? After capping the range, we can sample any distribution within that range, such as a log-uniform distribution. 

After generating simulated posteriors for over 10,000 pairs of these two onset parameters, I reviewed them manually one by one to build intuition, then generated summary statistics on the distribution of possible outcomes. I smoothed the numbers to generate the final digits for all values in the range. A direct average of models would be approximately 0.03 in 2026. The probability of the outcome for all values in 2026 is 0.01 and eventually grows to reasonably likely values by the end of 2030.อื่นๆassistant

Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
